controls.statement: User-centric service-level indicators are defined.
SLOs cover the most important availability, latency, correctness, durability, freshness, and quality outcomes.
SLOs are approved by product and engineering stakeholders.
SLO measurement represents actual user experience.
An error-budget policy controls release and reliability decisions.
The service is within its permitted error budget before a risky launch.
Critical dependencies have reliability expectations compatible with the product SLO.
Dependency reliability limitations are engineered around where necessary.
Every network call has an appropriate timeout.
Retries are bounded.
Retries use exponential backoff and jitter where appropriate.
Retried operations are safe or idempotent.
Circuit breakers or equivalent controls prevent cascading failure.
Bulkheads or isolation prevent one workload from exhausting all capacity.
Fallback behavior is defined and tested.
Graceful degradation prioritizes critical functionality.
Failure in optional functionality does not unnecessarily fail the whole product.
Health checks distinguish process liveness from readiness to serve.
Instances stop receiving work before shutdown.
In-flight work is completed, transferred, or safely retried during shutdown.
Redundancy crosses the failure domains it is intended to survive.
Shared control planes, identity systems, networks, storage, DNS, and providers are included in failure analysis.
Single points of failure are removed or explicitly accepted.
Network delay, packet loss, partitions, and DNS failure have been tested.
Dependency timeout, malformed response, throttling, and outage have been tested.
Cache outage and cache stampede behavior have been tested.
Database failover and replication lag have been tested.
Queue backlog and broker failure have been tested.
Disk-full, memory pressure, CPU exhaustion, file-descriptor exhaustion, and connection exhaustion have been tested.
Clock skew and time-service failure have been considered.
Certificate and key expiry have been considered.
Scheduled jobs handle overlapping or missed execution.
Stateful failover preserves required integrity.
Recovery does not create uncontrolled retry or traffic surges.
Maintenance and degraded modes are documented.
Controlled fault-injection or equivalent resilience tests have been completed for high-risk paths.
Recovery time from tested failures meets the approved objective.
Infrastructure is defined as code or otherwise reproducible and auditable.
Infrastructure changes receive review.
Infrastructure code is tested and security-scanned.
Production accounts, subscriptions, projects, and clusters are separated appropriately.
Resource ownership and criticality are labeled.
Operating systems, runtimes, database engines, and platform versions are supported.
Security patches are current according to risk policy.
Unnecessary services, packages, ports, and capabilities are removed.
Workloads run with the least operating-system and platform privilege.
Administrative access uses strong authentication and controlled entry points.
Just-in-time or time-bounded administrative access is used where practical.
Network segmentation and private connectivity are configured as designed.
Storage encryption and access policies are correct.
Critical resources have deletion protection or equivalent safeguards.
Resource quotas and account limits are documented.
Monitoring covers platform control-plane and quota failures.
Configuration drift and unauthorized resources are detected.
Asset inventory matches deployed infrastructure.
Production resource deletion and recreation have tested recovery procedures.
Multi-zone or multi-region architecture matches the required recovery and availability objectives.
Infrastructure capacity has been validated under failure.
Cloud or platform provider status and escalation paths are integrated into operations.
Infrastructure cost alerts and runaway-resource protections exist.
Break-glass access works during identity or network failure and is audited.
Infrastructure credentials and machine identities are rotated and inventoried.
Base images are minimal, trusted, pinned, and scanned.
Workloads do not run as root unless justified.
Filesystems are read-only where practical.
Unnecessary Linux or equivalent capabilities are removed.
Privileged containers and host access are prohibited unless explicitly approved.
Resource requests and limits are configured.
Runtime security policies are enforced.
Platform role-based access follows least privilege.
Network policies restrict unnecessary communication.
Admission or policy checks prevent prohibited workloads.
Image signatures or provenance are verified.
Secrets are not embedded in images.
Node, cluster, and control-plane upgrades have been rehearsed.
Eviction, rescheduling, and rolling-update behavior are tested.
Persistent-volume failure and restoration are tested.
Concurrency limits and scaling behavior are understood.

controls.statement: Log-injection and control-character attacks are handled.

controls.statement: Audit records identify actor, tenant, operation, target, time, source, outcome, and reason where appropriate.

controls.statement: Authentication, authorization changes, administrative actions, sensitive reads, exports, deletion, and configuration changes are audited.
heading_trail: 29. Observability, logging, metrics, and audit trails

controls.statement: Audit data is protected against unauthorized modification and deletion.
heading_trail: 29. Observability, logging, metrics, and audit trails

controls.statement: Audit access is restricted and audited.

controls.statement: Log and audit retention matches security, privacy, legal, and operational requirements.

controls.statement: Sampling does not discard critical security or correctness events.

controls.statement: Telemetry backlog and quota exhaustion are monitored.

controls.statement: Observability cost and cardinality are controlled without losing essential signals.

controls.statement: Alerts are tied to user impact, SLO risk, data integrity, security, or impending capacity failure.
Paging alerts are actionable.
Non-actionable information is sent through non-paging channels.
Alert severity definitions are documented.
Every alert has an owner.
Every page has a corresponding diagnostic or mitigation runbook.
Alert routing and escalation have been tested.
Primary and secondary coverage exist during required service hours.
On-call responders have the required access and tools.
No alert depends on one irreplaceable person.
Burn-rate or equivalent alerts detect both fast and slow SLO consumption.
Alert thresholds avoid obvious noise and missed incidents.
Duplicate alerts are correlated or suppressed appropriately.
Maintenance and deployments do not suppress unrelated incidents.
Failure of the monitoring or paging system generates an independent signal.
Runbooks include symptoms, impact, diagnosis, containment, rollback, recovery, verification, and escalation.
Runbooks avoid undocumented tribal knowledge.
Runbook commands are safe, reviewed, and clearly distinguish destructive actions.
Access to required dashboards and consoles works during an incident.
Provider support and escalation information is current.
Customer support knows how to escalate production problems.
A public or customer-facing status mechanism exists where appropriate.
On-call load and alert volume are operationally sustainable.
Handover procedures preserve active incident context.
On-call and runbook drills have been completed.
Security requirements are traceable to the threat model and recognized verification criteria.
The release is assessed against the applicable OWASP ASVS 5.0.0 requirements.
Source-code security analysis has run.
Dependency and SBOM analysis has run.
Secret scanning has run.
Infrastructure and configuration analysis has run.
Container or system-image analysis has run where applicable.
Deployed application security testing has run.
API security testing has run.
Authentication and recovery testing has run.
Authorization and tenant-isolation testing has run.
Injection and unsafe-input testing has run.
Browser and session security testing has run.
File-processing security testing has run where applicable.
Business-logic and abuse testing has run.
Manual code review covers the highest-risk components.
Independent penetration testing is complete where warranted.
Penetration testing includes authenticated users, multiple roles, multiple tenants, APIs, administrative tools, and business logic as applicable.
False positives are documented with evidence.
Findings have owners and remediation targets.
Fixed findings have been retested.
Relevant known-exploited vulnerabilities are treated as priority blockers unless exposure and mitigation are convincingly demonstrated.
Unsupported software and unpatchable components have explicit treatment plans.
Compensating controls are validated in the deployed environment.
A safe emergency-patching path exists.
External attack-surface discovery is continuous.
A vulnerability-disclosure policy and reporting channel exist.
Security reports receive acknowledgment, triage, remediation, disclosure, and credit processes as appropriate.
Customer security advisories can be produced promptly.
Security evidence is retained with the release.
Security regressions are represented in automated tests where practical.
Production security scanning is configured not to damage service or data.
Security monitoring covers account takeover, privilege changes, secret use, suspicious exports, abuse, and control tampering.
A current incident-response plan exists.
Incident severity levels are defined.
Authority to declare an incident is clear.
Incident roles include command, technical response, communications, documentation, security, privacy/legal, and business ownership as needed.
Primary and alternate communication channels exist.
Contact details are current and available during identity, network, or provider failure.
Procedures cover detection, triage, containment, eradication, recovery, and closure.
Procedures distinguish outages, security incidents, privacy incidents, safety events, and fraud events.
Evidence-preservation and forensic procedures exist.
Logging and time synchronization support investigation.
Credentials, sessions, certificates, and keys can be revoked or rotated rapidly.
Compromised builds and dependencies can be identified and replaced.
Customer and public communications templates exist.
A status-page process exists where appropriate.
Regulatory, contractual, insurer, partner, and law-enforcement notification requirements are mapped.
Notification deadlines and decision owners are documented.
Provider and subprocessor incident contacts are current.
Alternate operations are possible during provider failure.
Tabletop exercises cover realistic scenarios.
Exercises include account takeover, data exfiltration, destructive access, ransomware, dependency compromise, regional outage, and data corruption as relevant.
Exercise findings have owners and deadlines.
Post-incident reviews are blameless but accountable.
Corrective actions are tracked to completion.
Lessons are converted into tests, controls, runbooks, and architecture changes.
Incident metrics include detection, acknowledgment, containment, recovery, impact, and recurrence.
Incident records preserve decisions and timelines.
The plan can operate when the normal identity, chat, email, documentation, or cloud platform is unavailable.
Business-impact analysis identifies critical services and data.
Recovery Point Objective is defined for each stateful system.
Recovery Time Objective is defined for each critical journey.
Backup scope includes databases, files, queues where needed, configuration, infrastructure definitions, secrets or recovery mechanisms, certificates, and required artifacts.
Backups run automatically at the required frequency.
Backup success is monitored.
Backups are encrypted.
Backup access follows least privilege.
Backup copies are isolated from ordinary production compromise.
Immutable or otherwise tamper-resistant copies exist where risk warrants.
Retention meets operational, legal, contractual, and privacy requirements.
Backup keys and recovery credentials are protected.
Point-in-time recovery is available where required.
Full restoration has been tested.
Partial restoration has been tested.
Restoration to a clean environment has been tested.
Regional or provider-loss recovery has been tested when part of the design.
Restore order and dependency requirements are documented.
DNS, certificates, secrets, identity, networking, and external integrations are included in the recovery procedure.
Restored data is checked for integrity and reconciliation.
Actual tested recovery time meets the objective.
Failover and failback are both tested.
Disaster-recovery capacity can carry the required load.
Recovery does not accidentally send duplicate notifications, charges, webhooks, or jobs.
Backup restoration does not re-enable revoked users, secrets, or deleted data without detection.
Privacy deletion and backup-retention interactions are documented.
A ransomware or destructive-administrator scenario has been exercised.
Recovery does not depend on a single person or unavailable device.
Continuity procedures cover customer support, communications, and essential manual operations.
Recovery tests produce retained evidence and corrective actions.
The deployment plan identifies exact artifacts and target environments.
The plan identifies migrations, configuration changes, infrastructure changes, flags, and external dependencies.
Required approvals are complete.
Deployment permissions are restricted.
The person deploying cannot silently substitute an unapproved artifact.
Predeployment checks validate environment health and capacity.
Required backups or recovery points exist.
Database migration steps and ordering are explicit.
Application, worker, scheduled-job, and schema compatibility is maintained during rollout.
Mixed-version operation is tested where it will occur.
Deployment uses a progressive, canary, blue-green, cohort, or similarly controlled approach where risk warrants.
The smallest safe initial cohort is used.
Automated health gates examine user-facing success, latency, errors, saturation, and business integrity.
Canary and control populations are comparable.
Rollout pauses automatically or operationally on defined signals.
